extracted.intended_audience: CRTC commissioners, Commission counsel, CRTC staff, and regulatory policymakers/practitioners in broadcasting and telecommunications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and recommended procedural standards for how the CRTC should run public hearings and process broadcasting and telecommunications applications, including delegation, cross-examination, counsel roles, notice/disclosure, and application filing/processing rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation to committees and staff
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act obviously foresaw the need for delegation of the Executive Committee's functions to smaller committees and a mechanism was provided for this. The Commission has set up, in addition to the two bodies mentioned above, standing committees in the broadcasting area to perform such functions as reviewing applications in order to determine the agenda and scheduling of hearings, determining which applications require oral hearings, deciding certain applications and overseeing research activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: expand authority to delegate some hearing responsibilities to senior staff officers (as already done to some extent on the telecommunications side). Examples under section 81 of the National Transportation Act: appoint staff officers to conduct pre-hearing conferences, sit on panels in regional hearings, act as taxing officers, make inquiries on disputes. Staff officers could hold inquiries and make reports to Commissioners on programming complaints and routine licence amendment applications; their reports would become part of the file material on which Commissioners base decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure Commissioners' availability; delegate to free time
rubrics_metrics.description: For a committee system to work effectively, Commissioners must be available for meetings. The inordinate demands on Commissioners' time made by the hearing schedule can make it difficult to convene meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider delegating some hearing responsibilities to senior staff officers to free Commissioners for committee work and decision-making on broadcasting applications. Use of delegation is a practical response to heavy hearing loads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-examination policy in adversarial cases
rubrics_metrics.description: In applications where there is a real contest between parties and substantial interests are at stake, the Commission should adopt more strictly a role of pure adjudicator and allow the parties to thoroughly test each other's evidence and positions through cross-examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the informal debating format encourages public participation, it 'has not lent itself to a searching examination of the evidence.' Recommendation: in any application involving parties whose positions are clearly adversarial, the Commission should routinely permit, upon request by any such party, the right of cross-examination. Pre-hearing procedures (timely requests and showing of warrant) should not impose an unduly heavy onus that prevents cross-examination where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pre-hearing conferences to resolve procedural/cross-examination issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rules of Procedure (s.29) provide for pre-hearing conferences for purposes such as the simplification of issues and settling of procedures in order to expedite hearings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: make more frequent use of informal pre-hearing conferences presided over by the designated Chair or counsel to assist in resolving questions of cross-examination and other procedural issues prior to the hearing. Pre-hearing conferences help determine whether an adversarial or informal approach is appropriate given the subject matter and interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the Commission's counsel and designation of lead questioner
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike some tribunals where counsel acts solely as legal advisor, the CRTC's counsel has traditionally taken an active role in questioning at public hearings, although practice has shifted so Commissioners begin questioning and counsel finishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-appraise counsel's role: where matters are complex, procedural or legal, or where an adversarial stance is desired, counsel should have primary responsibility for questioning and be permitted to take the lead. Where Commissioners should ask questions, the Chairman should designate a Commissioner to be the lead questioner well in advance so they can study files and develop lines of questioning. Make counsel and appropriate staff available to (part-time and full-time) Commissioners for preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality, planning and focus of questioning at hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of the questioning at CRTC broadcasting hearings is extremely important; because parties are not usually permitted to question each other, an important burden falls on the Commission to ask all the questions that are relevant and necessary to fully expose and test the position of each party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid loose, disorganized, random questioning that lacks specificity and follow-through. Questioning should be planned and logical, cover issues in sufficient depth, and be designed to clarify or discredit conflicting statements. Poorly planned questioning leads to incomplete records, may harm decision quality and the Commission's credibility. Designate lead questioner and prepare thoroughly in advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of the issues in public hearing notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Public notice used by the Commission generally contains a brief description of the applications, place of hearing and instructions on intervening; there is rarely mention of the issues that caused the Commission to call a hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: where appropriate, include a statement of the matters of particular concern to the Commission in the notice (section 27 requires at least ten days' notice to an applicant stating whether they must appear). Adequate notice focuses discussion, eliminates surprises, allows parties to prepare and ensures fairer hearings. Recognize cases where stating issues in advance is not appropriate (e.g., mere fact of competition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of staff evidence and briefing materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Working paper distinguishes two categories of staff documents: (1) documents that add evidence (e.g., staff reports on inspections and program analyses) and (2) documents that summarize applications and discuss relevance of regulations/policies (not adding evidence). The paper suggested the first category should be disclosed and the second kept confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: disclose all briefing materials prepared for Commissioners prior to the hearing, including summaries and staff perceptions/questions, in sufficient time to enable parties to comment on any errors or omissions. Rationale: Commissioners (especially part-time) rely on briefing materials; disclosure helps focus discussion, eliminate surprises, correct factual errors in time (avoids wasted hearing time) and improve fairness. Confidentiality procedures should remain for legitimately confidential information, but disclosure should be the norm where the document informs the Commission's line of questioning or factual reliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting statutory criteria in telecommunications decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory tests of justness, reasonableness and non-discrimination in relation to tolls and services are narrower in scope than Broadcasting Act provisions, but the CRTC has interpreted these statutory criteria in a broad fashion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission links 'justness and reasonableness' to the quality of services, extends 'non-discrimination' to relationships with customers and suppliers, and considers public policy consequences (effects on autonomy, availability/expansion of services, competition). Where legislation provides no guidance (e.g., interconnection agreements), the Commission should identify relevant public interest tests (e.g., effect on powers/autonomy, availability/expansion of services, competition) and apply them, recognizing the burden and complexity of doing so without explicit government policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codified procedures for telecommunications proceedings (interrogatories, confidentiality, registration)
rubrics_metrics.description: The CRTC published telecommunications Rules of Procedure that codified practices and introduced innovations (right to submit interrogatories, full procedure for confidentiality claims, registration for interested parties to be served with copies of certain applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the codified procedures: allow interrogatories in various proceedings and require applicants to respond; implement a full confidentiality-claim procedure for handling sensitive material; enable interested parties to register with the Secretary to receive materials. These procedural rules are tailored to telecommunications applications and are intended to increase transparency and orderly processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights and types of intervention in general rate increase proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Notices set out three methods of intervention: send a letter of comment, make a submission at a regional hearing (in addition to or instead of a letter), or fully participate in the central hearing by filing a 'notice of intention to participate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tiered intervention process accommodates various classes of interested persons according to their desired involvement. Expect that extent of participation varies inversely with time and resources required. Rules also subdivide intervention types for other proceedings and include entitlement to costs in general rate increase proceedings with a method for taxation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application content requirements for general rate increase filings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rules provide that the general rate increase application must be in two parts: (1) material formerly filed (letter) accompanied by a table showing present and proposed rates; and (2) supporting memoranda containing all evidence and exhibits intended to be introduced at the hearing, describing progress and status of outstanding matters from the most recent Commission decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: permit interveners to know the applicant's entire case at the outset, better assess whether to intervene, identify interrogatories, and save hearing time because evidence-in-chief can be tabled and updated rather than led through witnesses. Applicants should include detailed supporting memoranda and full exhibits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public notice requirements for general rate increase applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Following filing of an application, extensive public notice is required. The Rules provide for a simplified form of notice spelling out the changes applied for and the reasons for them to be published in newspapers of general circulation specified by the Commission in the territory served by the applicant. Applicants must also mail a similar notice to each telephone subscriber. Copies of the application and the Commission's directions on procedure are required to be placed in each of the company's business offices for public inspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In addition to general-public notices, persons registered as 'interested parties' must be served with all material filed by the applicant. The notices must also explain the methods of intervention available. These measures ensure broad public awareness and enable meaningful participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrogatories: rights to ask and obligations to answer
rubrics_metrics.description: After filing interventions, anyone who has filed a notice of intention to participate may address interrogatories to the applicant. Interrogatories are questions put in writing on any aspect of the application. Under the Rules, the applicant is required to respond to all interrogatories furnished to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the applicant is unable or unwilling to furnish a full and adequate response because the information is not relevant, unavailable, or confidential, the applicant must supply full reasons supporting these grounds. Interrogatories have traditionally been numerous and wide-ranging; the Rules require applicants to answer or justify non-disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processing of tariff page applications and Tariff Committee practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Tariff changes are made by filing letters that include the proposed new tariff page, reasons for the changes and any supporting documentation. These filings are reviewed by the Telecommunications Branch and a Tariff Committee (sub-committee of the Executive Committee) which meets regularly to review filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The majority of tariff filings are approved and an order issued shortly after. Those the Committee judges should have public exposure are handled by public notice calling for comments, usually within thirty days. After comments, the Commission may hold a public hearing or decide on the written record.
